Symbolic MRD interfaces with an RC11-style axiomatic model but refines its dependency relation (dp), removing false dependencies so that load→store reorderings in load-buffering shapes — e.g. the LB+UB+data outcome RC11 forbids because of a cycle in ⊑∪rf — become allowed, while genuine out-of-thin-air cycles stay forbidden. It therefore admits strictly more behaviours than RC11.
Both are language-level models providing DRF-SC but with different treatments of racy accesses.

Both are multi-copy atomic and coincide on every standard litmus family over the common instruction set (verified against herd7's aarch64.cat and riscv.cat). The incomparability is instruction-level: RISC-V's fence.tso (which allows SB) and the RCsc/RCpc atomics differ from ARMv8's. See litmus/incomparable/ARMv8-vs-RVWMO.

Both halves decided by memalloy over the common Basic_HW fragment, as for TSO → ARMv8. memalloy ships no RISC-V model, so the operand is litmus/memalloy/models/zoo_hw_rvwmo.cat, authored here directly from the thirteen ppo rules of the RVWMO chapter of the RISC-V unprivileged spec; the file annotates each rule it renders and each that is empty on the fragment. Witness at 4 events; containment clean exhaustively to 7. Independent check on the rendering: over the same fragment it is contained in the ARMv8 operand and ARMv8 is not contained in it, which is the direction the same-address ppo rules predict. Bounded evidence about that rendering, not a theorem about RVWMO.

IMM compiles correctly to ARMv8. Machine-checked with kater: imm::psc ⊆ arm8::ob*, the mapping's soundness condition, under the well-formedness premise rf;rmw ⊆ mo (litmus/kater/queries/compilation-IMM-vs-ARMv8.kat) — the paper's Table 1 query, reproduced here.

IMM compiles correctly to x86-TSO. Machine-checked with kater: imm::psc ⊆ tso::tso* over kater's imm.kat and tso.kat (litmus/kater/queries/compilation-IMM-vs-x86-TSO.kat). kater's tso.kat is the TSO rendering; it carries to the x86-TSO node along the by-construction TSO ≡ x86-TSO equivalence edge.
IMM compiles correctly to POWER.

Containment proved by kater, unbounded: each of LKMM's three global ordering axioms — acyclic(hb), the prop;ppo* work-around, and coherence — follows from SC's acyclic(sc). The operand is not kater's kat/lkmm2.kat, which is written over internal (-imm) relations and does not load in any mode; it is the mechanical restatement over kater's builtin theory that litmus/kater/derive-lkmm.sh generates, so the proof is about that rendering. Query: litmus/kater/queries/strictly-weaker-SC-vs-LKMM.kat. Strictness stays with the witness: LKMM permits reorderings of plain and *_ONCE accesses (e.g. store-buffering, SB) that SC forbids; DRF-style synchronisation must be requested explicitly with smp_mb() and friends. See litmus/strictly-weaker/SC-vs-LKMM.

Neither contains the other: LKMM provides RCU grace-period ordering and the smp_* barrier family with no C11 counterpart, while C11 offers per-object seq_cst atomics LKMM does not model. The incomparability is at the level of primitives, not reorderings of shared operations. See litmus/incomparable/C11-vs-LKMM.

Lahav, Giannarakis & Vafeiadis, POPL 2016: SRA has exactly the same compilation scheme to x86-TSO as the RA fragment it strengthens — plain loads and stores, no fences — so the strengthening carries no implementation cost on x86.

Lahav, Giannarakis & Vafeiadis, POPL 2016: SRA compiles to POWER by the standard RA scheme (lwsync before every store, ctrl+isync after every load), and the mapping is complete as well as sound — the compiled program exhibits exactly the behaviours of the source. Lahav & Boker restate it as SRA precisely coinciding with the POWER model of Alglave et al. restricted to programs compiled from the RA fragment. Completeness is what makes SRA maximal: it cannot be strengthened further without an implementation cost on POWER.
Linux kernel primitives compile correctly to x86; LKMM is designed to be no stronger than the hardware it runs on.
Linux kernel primitives compile correctly to ARMv8/AArch64.
Linux kernel primitives compile correctly to IBM POWER.
Linux kernel primitives compile correctly to RISC-V (RVWMO).

OpenCL 2.0 extends C11 with memory scopes; at all-SVM-devices scope it coincides with C11, but narrower scopes (work-group, device) permit synchronisation-free weak behaviours that flat C11 forbids. See Batty, Donaldson & Wickerson (POPL 2016).
CUDA's cuda::atomic mirrors C++11 atomics but adds thread scopes (block, device, system); sub-system scopes admit behaviours C11 forbids.
HRF generalises DRF to a scope hierarchy; restricted to a single global scope it matches C11's DRF-SC guarantee, while sub-global scopes admit additional weak behaviours.
Gaster et al.'s HRF-Relaxed loosens HRF-direct/indirect's exact scope-matching, admitting more programs and behaviours than the original HRF models.
Both are scoped release-consistency ISA models, but expose different scope sets (CTA/GPU/system vs HSA work-group/agent/system) and cache-control qualifiers; neither subsumes the other.

NVIDIA Tile IR docs §7: 'The axioms and relations of the Tile IR memory model are intended to be a strict weakening of the PTX memory model.' Vendor-asserted (note the hedged 'intended to be' language); not independently proven or machine-checked.
Both are scoped GPU API models, but differ in scope sets and synchronisation primitives — Vulkan adds explicit availability/visibility operations that OpenCL lacks; neither contains the other.
CUDA C++ atomics lower to PTX; the CUDA model is layered directly on the PTX memory model.

OpenCL kernels compile to PTX on NVIDIA GPUs. Verified sound by memalloy: no execution where the compiled PTX behaviour violates the source OpenCL semantics, up to 4 OpenCL / 6 PTX events (opencl_scoped -> ptx_orig via the opencl_ptx mapping); the known-buggy mapping variant yields a counterexample at 5 events, confirming the check discriminates. Reproduced via litmus/memalloy/ (Docker).
OpenCL kernels compile to AMD's GPU ISA via the HSA-based model.
Vulkan/SPIR-V compute shaders compile to PTX on NVIDIA GPUs.
Vulkan/SPIR-V compute shaders compile to AMD's GPU ISA.
Browser WebGPU implementations lower WGSL to Vulkan (and to Metal/Direct3D 12); the WGSL model is derived from Vulkan's.
On Apple platforms WebGPU implementations lower WGSL to Metal.

Both yield only sequentially consistent outcomes for data-race-free programs. DRFx additionally gives racy programs catch-fire semantics — a runtime raises an exception when it detects a region-bounded data race — so the survey groups it with SC rather than weakening the behaviour of well-synchronised code.
BMM equips each thread with a store buffer, so the store→load (SB) outcome becomes observable; SC forbids it.
BMM is a pragmatic TSO-style buffered model proposed as a candidate Java memory model; on the store-buffer relaxations it coincides with TSO.
Like PSO, RMMOA's hierarchical store buffers additionally permit store→store reordering to distinct addresses, which TSO forbids.
RMMOA is an operational model whose out-of-order propagation of writes to different locations matches PSO's store→store relaxation.

RA is the release/acquire fragment of the C/C++11 model — release stores, acquire reads, acquire-release RMWs (Lahav & Boker, §3.1). RC11's repairs concern the SC axioms and the relaxed/thin-air fragment, none of which this fragment contains, so RC11 and C11 coincide on it. Drawn against RC11 rather than C11 to match the existing PSI and SI compilation notes, which target 'the release-acquire (RA) fragment of RC11'.
RAR is an operational reformulation of RC11's release-acquire and relaxed fragment, used as the basis for an invariant-based proof calculus.
ORC11 is an operational version of RC11 developed for RustBelt to verify Rust standard-library synchronisation primitives against a program logic.

CRC is a compositional semantics for a thin-air-free fragment of C11 (non-atomics with catch-fire, release-acquire, SC fences); by omitting relaxed atomics it forbids the out-of-thin-air behaviours plain C11 permits.
JAM borrows RC11's OOTA fix for opaque and stronger accesses, but unlike RC11 it does not tackle thin-air for plain (non-atomic) accesses, so it permits more behaviours.

JAM is a proposed revision of the JMM built on VarHandle access modes (plain/opaque/release-acquire/volatile); it strengthens the treatment of atomics via RC11 while differing from the original JMM's causality machinery, so neither contains the other.

OHMM is an operational attempt to repair the JMM — a global event buffer with a replay mechanism, tracking syntactic dependencies to forbid thin-air. It restructures the JMM's semantics rather than strictly refining it, so the two are incomparable.

Both are syntactic-dependency-preserving models that forbid thin-air by respecting syntactic dependencies, but over different primitives (Linux-kernel barriers vs a JMM-style happens-before machine); neither subsumes the other.

Weakestmo grounds thin-air reads with event structures and is, in the authors' words, 'stronger than C11 (which allows OOTA) and weaker than RC11': every separating outcome (the OOTA load-buffering test and the 'RNG' bogus-value example) is allowed by C11 and forbidden by Weakestmo, with no behaviour Weakestmo allows that C11 forbids. So C11 is strictly weaker. (Reclassified from incomparable; see litmus/strictly-weaker/Weakestmo-vs-C11.)

Both are semantic-dependency-preserving models that forbid out-of-thin-air, admit the optimal compilation mappings, and give external DRF. Weakestmo is built on event structures (vs Promising's promises/certification) and, unlike the Promising semantics, supports sequentially consistent accesses; neither is a subset of the other.

CSRA pairs a POWER-inspired memory subsystem with per-thread event structures and permits optimisation while avoiding thin-air. Its authors state CSRA is a subset of C/C++11 by design ('the converse is not to be expected ... the point of our model is to exclude the thin-air executions that C/C++11 allows'): only out-of-thin-air outcomes separate them, all allowed by C11 and forbidden by CSRA. So C11 is strictly weaker. (Reclassified from incomparable; see litmus/strictly-weaker/CSRA-vs-C11.)

Both are semantic-dependency-preserving models avoiding thin-air; CSRA's compilation to x86 and POWER is sound, but unlike Promising its mappings to ARMv7/ARMv8 were later shown non-optimal. Neither contains the other.

WJES uses a game-semantics-inspired notion of well-justification to forbid thin-air and prove external DRF. A load→load reordering counterexample shows its mappings to ARMv7/ARMv8/POWER are not optimal, so it is incomparable with C11.

Leaky Semicolon §9: 'PwT-mca is incomparable to both RC11 ... and the promising semantics'. RC11 allows non-multi-copy-atomic behaviours that PwT-mca disallows, while PwT-mca allows optimisations that RC11's No-Thin-Air axiom forbids.
Leaky Semicolon §9: 'PwT-mca is incomparable to both RC11 ... and the promising semantics [Kang et al. 2017] ... PwT-mca has a weaker notion of coherence than the promising semantics.'

Leaky Semicolon §9/App. E: 'PwT-mca generalizes PwP to account for sequential composition'; PwP imposes m7c (reads-from implies pomset order) and 'is similar to PwT-mca1', whereas 'PwT-mca2 ... drops ... m7c' and 'is a weaker model new to this paper' (§4.2). Dropping m7c admits behaviours PwP forbids: the Arm8 execution of §4.2 is allowed by PwT-mca2 but 'disallowed by PwT-mca1', witnessing that the LeakySemi/PwT-mca model is strictly weaker (more permissive) than PwP. Since PwP is roughly PwT-mca1 rather than exactly it (§9: 'PwT is based on PwP, [but] there are many differences'), no equivalence is claimed.

GOS gives a generative operational semantics with stratification constraints on speculation to rule out thin-air values and prove external DRF; it forbids thin-air reads C11 permits but is not a strict subset.

The JavaScript model is based on C11 and shares its thin-air problem (only internal DRF), but — unlike C11 — it does not treat racy non-atomic accesses as undefined behaviour and it natively supports mixed-size accesses over SharedArrayBuffer. Neither contains the other.

Watt et al. 2019 §7.2 / Fig. 20 give the compilation of C/C++11 accesses to Wasm memory accesses, mapping all C/C++ atomics (relaxed, acquire/release, seq_cst) onto Wasm seqcst atomics; the sketch shows the compiled program is SC-DRF and thus behaviourally correct at the level of memory accesses.

Watt et al. 2019 §6.3 (Prop. 6.2): dropping Wasm's two strengthening conditions (†,‡) yields exactly the consistency behaviours of the (uncorrected) JavaScript model on shared array buffers. The paper proposes adding (†,‡) to JavaScript as a strict strengthening; TC39 adopted them, and the repaired model is this dataset's JSMM — so full Wasm and JSMM agree on the shared-memory data-access (SharedArrayBuffer) fragment (excluding traps, memory growth, and mixed-size beyond the shared subset).

Watt et al. 2019 Fig. 19 tabulates the compilation of Wasm memory accesses to x86 (whose ISA model is TSO), following the established C/C++11 SC-atomic schemes [Sewell & Sevcik 2016]; full mixed-size correctness is flagged as an open problem (§7.1.1).

Watt et al. 2019 Fig. 19 gives the compilation of Wasm memory accesses to ARMv7, following the established C/C++11 SC-atomic schemes [Sewell & Sevcik 2016]; full mixed-size correctness is flagged as an open problem (§7.1.1).

Watt et al. 2019 Fig. 19 gives the compilation of Wasm memory accesses to AArch64/ARMv8 (LDR/STR, LDAR/STLR), following the established C/C++11 SC-atomic schemes [Sewell & Sevcik 2016]; full mixed-size correctness is flagged as an open problem (§7.1.1).

The Relaxed Memory Calculus specifies ordering constraints directly in source code rather than deriving them from access annotations. It is very weak and permits thin-air values (only internal DRF is proved); its primitives differ from C11's, so the two are incomparable.

RAO explains relaxed behaviour via transformations over an SC execution. Its authors claim external DRF while still permitting thin-air values — two properties known to be incompatible in general (Batty et al., ESOP 2015) — which the survey attributes to restrictions on the input language (no general conditionals). Incomparable with C11.

TSC is a general framework for the effects of speculative execution. Under unrestricted speculation the external DRF theorem fails (only internal DRF holds) and thin-air values appear; it studies speculation abstractly rather than refining C11, so the two are incomparable.

EtE-SC restores end-to-end sequential consistency via an SC-preserving LLVM compiler and modified x86 hardware; it admits exactly the SC outcomes, differing from SC only in enforcement mechanism and performance, not in allowed behaviours.

Volatile-by-default makes every Java access sequentially consistent, so it admits exactly the SC outcomes; it differs from SC only in enforcement mechanism (speculative JIT recompilation) and performance.

SC-Haskell preserves sequential consistency using Haskell's type system to separate thread-local from shared mutable state; it admits exactly the SC outcomes, differing from SC only in mechanism and performance.

The paper states DeNovo provides sequential consistency for data-race-free programs, so on the race-free fragment it admits exactly the SC outcomes. Unlike DRFx it assumes race-freedom is supplied by the disciplined language (Deterministic Parallel Java) rather than detected at runtime, and defines no behaviour for racy programs.

Sung, Komuravelli & Adve (DeNovoND, ASPLOS 2013) state their disciplined-non-determinism (lock-based) design guarantees sequential consistency, so on the data-race-free fragment it admits exactly the SC outcomes. Like DeNovo it assumes software supplies race-freedom and defines no behaviour for racy programs; the value-add over DeNovo is the coherence design (locks / access signatures), not the consistency class.

Sung & Adve (DeNovoSync, ASPLOS 2015) adopt the standard C++/Java data-race-free memory model, which defines sequentially consistent semantics for data-race-free programs (SC is used as the correctness criterion for synchronization accesses), so on the race-free fragment it admits exactly the SC outcomes. It extends DeNovo to arbitrary synchronization while keeping this SC-for-DRF contract.

Alsop, Sinclair & Adve (Spandex, ISCA 2018) state they assume a sequential-consistency-for-data-race-free (SC-for-DRF) model, so on the race-free fragment it admits exactly the SC outcomes; the flexible coherence request types affect only performance, not the consistency guarantee.
Sequential consistency is strictly stronger than processor consistency (Goodman 1989; Steinke & Nutt 2004).
Causal memory is strictly weaker than sequential consistency (Ahamad et al. 1995; Steinke & Nutt 2004).

SRA is the strongest of the release-acquire family and is still strictly weaker than SC: Lahav & Boker Ex. 3.5 marks the IRIW outcome allowed under WRA, RA and SRA alike, and SC forbids it. Store buffering is likewise allowed — SRA's compilation to x86-TSO uses plain accesses. The SRA paper supplies fences that restore sequential consistency, which is only meaningful because the model without them is weaker.

SRA replaces RA's write-coherence (mo;hb irreflexive — a local agreement between modification order and happens-before) with strong-write-coherence ((hb ∪ mo)+ irreflexive — a global one), keeping RA's other axioms (Lahav & Boker, Table 1); containment is immediate. Strictness is the 2+2W program of Lahav et al. 2016, Lahav & Boker Ex. 3.6: x:=1; y:=2; a:=y || y:=1; x:=2; b:=x with a=b=1. The outcome forces mo edges W(y,2) -> W(y,1) and W(x,2) -> W(x,1), closing an (hb ∪ mo) cycle that SRA forbids while each mo;hb step alone satisfies write-coherence, so RA allows it. Machine-checked: litmus/models/ra.cat and litmus/models/sra.cat are authored for this dataset and differ in that one axiom, and litmus/strictly-weaker/SRA-vs-RA/ runs 2+2W under both (Sometimes 1 8 vs Never 0 5). Because both cat models are hand-written rather than vendored, the directory also carries controls run by run.sh: MP+relacq must be forbidden by both, and IRIW must be allowed by both — the latter checked against Lahav & Boker Ex. 3.5, which marks IRIW allowed under RA and SRA alike. Containment remains the cited one-axiom argument; herd7 decides the strictness half only.

WRA drops modification order entirely, replacing RA's write-coherence and read-coherence with weak-read-coherence over hb|loc; Lahav & Boker note that write-coherence implies [W];hb|loc;[W] subset of mo, so read-coherence implies weak-read-coherence and RA contains WRA (Prop. 3.2). Strictness is Ex. 3.7, three single-location programs (WW, Oscillating, SF) allowed by WRA and forbidden by RA: WRA does not provide SC-per-location, so even one-location programs may behave non-sequentially.

Lahav & Boker, §3.1: ignoring RMWs, SRA is equivalent to the causal convergence model CCv of Bouajjani et al., applied to the standard sequential specification of a read/write key-value store (and to the causal consistency of Cerone et al. restricted to single-instruction transactions). fragment_restricted because the equivalence is stated modulo RMWs: SRA's atomicity axiom has no counterpart in a model over a sequential key-value specification. This edge is the bridge between the C11 family and the distributed causal-consistency cluster.
Lahav & Boker: WRA 'provides the most minimal guarantees required from a model to satisfy causal consistency; it is equivalent to the model called CC studied in' Bouajjani et al. (POPL 2017).

Bouajjani et al., POPL 2017, §4 and Fig. 1: CM and CCv 'are both strictly stronger than CC'. Witness: Fig. 2 history (2c) — pa: wr(x,1) || pb: wr(x,2); rd(x)▷1; rd(x)▷2 — is CC but neither CM nor CCv, since pb revises its ordering of the two writes after already having read one of them.

Bouajjani et al., POPL 2017, Lemma 2 (after Perrin et al.): every CCv history is CC, since AxArb gives co subset of arb and hence AxCausalArb implies AxCausalValue. Strictness is the same Fig. 2 history (2c), which is CC but not CCv.
Bouajjani et al., POPL 2017, Example 7: history (2d) satisfies CC, CM and CCv, yet admits no total order over all its operations, so it is not sequentially consistent.

Causal memory and causal convergence are incomparable (Perrin, Mostéfaoui & Jard, PPoPP 2016; Bouajjani et al., POPL 2017, §1 and Fig. 1). Both witnesses are in Bouajjani et al. Fig. 2. History (2a) — pa: wr(x,1); rd(x)▷2 || pb: wr(x,2); rd(x)▷1 — is CM but not CCv, because arbitration would have to place wr(x,2) both after and before wr(x,1) (Ex. 5). History (2b) — pa: wr(z,1); wr(x,1); wr(y,1) || pb: wr(x,2); rd(z)▷0; rd(y)▷1; rd(x)▷2 — is CCv but not CM: reading y=1 drags wr(z,1) into pb's causal past behind wr(x,2), which the earlier rd(z)▷0 contradicts (Ex. 6).
Processor consistency is strictly stronger than PRAM consistency (Goodman 1989; Steinke & Nutt 2004).
Processor consistency is strictly stronger than cache consistency (Goodman 1989; Steinke & Nutt 2004). The Coherence node is Goodman's cache consistency.
Causal memory is strictly stronger than PRAM consistency (Steinke & Nutt 2004).
Slow consistency is strictly weaker than PRAM consistency (Hutto & Ahamad 1990; Steinke & Nutt 2004).
Slow consistency is strictly weaker than cache consistency (Hutto & Ahamad 1990; Steinke & Nutt 2004).
Local consistency is the weakest model, strictly weaker than slow consistency (Bataller & Bernabeu-Auban 1997; Steinke & Nutt 2004).

Burckhardt, Gotsman, Yang & Zawirski, POPL 2014, §7: (cross-object) causal consistency imposes the ordering axioms COCV/COCA, while per-object causal consistency imposes only the weaker per-object axioms POCV/POCA over the per-object happens-before order (Viotti & Vukolić 2016, §3.9). COCV/COCA disallow strictly more anomalies, so cross-object causal consistency is strictly stronger than per-object causal consistency. Re-homed from the Causal node: Burckhardt's cross-object causal consistency is the visibility/arbitration one, i.e. CCv, not causal memory.

Burckhardt, Gotsman, Yang & Zawirski, POPL 2014, §7: an execution is per-object causally consistent iff it is eventually consistent (EVENTUAL+THINAIR) AND satisfies the per-object ordering axioms POCV/POCA. Adding those axioms disallows strictly more anomalies (e.g. Fig. 14(b), §3.1), so eventual consistency is strictly weaker than per-object causal consistency.

Causal+ = Causality ∧ StrongConvergence (Viotti & Vukolić 2016, Eq. 27; Lloyd et al., COPS, SOSP 2011). V-V's Causality (Eq. 26) is the visibility/arbitration causal consistency that Bouajjani et al. name CCv, so this containment is against CCv. Adding strong convergence disallows strictly more behaviours, so CCv is strictly weaker than causal+. Re-homed from the Causal node, where the same note had been read as a containment against causal memory.

RealTimeCausality = Causality ∧ RealTime (Viotti & Vukolić 2016, Eq. 28; Mahajan, Alvisi & Dahlin 2011). V-V's Causality (Eq. 26) is causal convergence, so this containment is against CCv. It adds RealTime (Eq. 9, rb ⊆ ar) — causally concurrent, real-time-non-overlapping writes must be applied in real-time order — disallowing strictly more behaviours, so CCv is strictly weaker than real-time causal consistency. Re-homed from the Causal node, where the same note had been read as a containment against causal memory.

Causal+ = CCv ∧ StrongConvergence, and CCv is incomparable to causal memory, so the two are incomparable rather than ordered. This replaces a strictly_weaker edge that read the Viotti-Vukolić containment (Eq. 27) as being against causal memory; it is against CCv. Witnesses, both Bouajjani et al. POPL 2017 Fig. 2: history (2a) is CM but not CCv, hence not causal+; history (2b) is CCv and not CM, and reads each of x, y and z exactly once, so StrongConvergence (V-V Eq. 17, constraining only reads with equal visible-write sets) is vacuous on it — it is causal+ but not CM.

RealTimeCausality = CCv ∧ RealTime, and CCv is incomparable to causal memory. This replaces a strictly_weaker edge that read the Viotti-Vukolić containment (Eq. 28) as being against causal memory; it is against CCv. Witnesses, both Bouajjani et al. POPL 2017 Fig. 2: history (2a) is CM but not CCv, hence not real-time causal; history (2b) is CCv and not CM, and admits a real-time schedule — pa's writes all completing before pb starts — whose arbitration order (pa's writes before wr(x,2)) extends rb, so RealTime (V-V Eq. 9, rb ⊆ ar) holds. RealTime constrains arbitration only, not visibility, so rd(z)▷0 may still miss wr(z,1): it is real-time causal but not CM.

Causal+ and real-time causal consistency are incomparable (Viotti & Vukolić 2016, §3.5): real-time causality does not imply strong convergence, and causal+ does not impose real-time ordering — each forbids a behaviour the other allows. (V-V correct Lloyd et al.'s original claim that real-time causal is stronger than causal+.)

Unlike the Causal edge to the same node, this one is a derivation rather than a citation. CCv is CausalVisibility ∧ CausalArbitration ∧ RVal (Viotti & Vukolić 2016, Eq. 26), where CausalArbitration is hb ⊆ ar and hb = (so ∪ vis)+. WritesFollowReads is (vis; so|rd→wr) ⊆ ar (Eq. 25). Since vis ⊆ hb and so ⊆ hb, the composite vis;so|rd→wr lies in hb+ = hb ⊆ ar, so CCv satisfies WFR by construction. The converse fails — WFR constrains only write-after-read within a session and says nothing about visibility or the arbitration of anything else — so writes-follow-reads is strictly weaker.

Brzezinski, Sobaniec & Wawrzyniak (PDP 2004) show that causal consistency requires all four session guarantees — read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads. Their data-centric models are the classical shared-memory taxonomy (atomic, sequential, causal, processor, PRAM, weak, release, scope, entry), so their causal consistency is causal memory, and this edge is correctly against the Causal node rather than CCv. Causal memory therefore implies writes-follow-reads while the converse fails — one session guarantee constrains far less than a per-site serialisation over the causal order — so writes-follow-reads is strictly weaker. Note this is an implication, not an equality: neither Brzezinski et al. nor Viotti & Vukolić state the converse here (see issue #11), and the earlier gloss 'causal = PRAM ∧ writes-follow-reads, Eq. 25' was wrong twice over — Eq. 25 is the definition of WritesFollowReads, not a theorem about causal consistency, and the sources assert only that causal consistency 'requires and includes them all'.

Brzezinski et al. (2003) proved PRAM consistency holds iff a system provides read-your-writes, monotonic reads and monotonic writes (Viotti & Vukolić 2016, Eq. 20). PRAM is the conjunction of the three, so it implies read-your-writes while the converse fails: read-your-writes is strictly weaker than PRAM.

Brzezinski et al. (2003) proved PRAM = read-your-writes ∧ monotonic reads ∧ monotonic writes (Viotti & Vukolić 2016, Eq. 20). PRAM implies monotonic reads while the converse fails, so monotonic reads is strictly weaker than PRAM.

Brzezinski et al. (2003) proved PRAM = read-your-writes ∧ monotonic reads ∧ monotonic writes (Viotti & Vukolić 2016, Eq. 20). PRAM implies monotonic writes while the converse fails, so monotonic writes is strictly weaker than PRAM.
Processor and causal consistency are incomparable: each forbids a behaviour the other allows (Steinke & Nutt 2004).
PRAM and cache consistency are incomparable: PRAM orders a process's own writes globally but not per-location, cache consistency the converse (Goodman 1989; Steinke & Nutt 2004).
Causal and cache consistency are incomparable (Steinke & Nutt 2004).

mca.note: Pulte et al. give ARMv8 an explicitly multicopy-atomic semantics — the revised architecture (and this paper's title) fixes each write to become visible to all other threads at a single point.
Pre-v8 ARM is non-multicopy-atomic; Pulte et al. adopt multicopy atomicity for ARMv8, explicitly departing from the earlier non-MCA ARM model.
POWER is the canonical non-multicopy-atomic architecture; Sarkar et al.'s operational storage-subsystem model lets a write propagate to different threads at different times.
x86-TSO places a single shared memory behind per-thread FIFO store buffers, so a store becomes visible to all other threads at once — multicopy atomic.
TSO's shared-memory-plus-store-buffer structure makes writes multicopy atomic (Owens et al., x86-TSO extended version).
The RISC-V RVWMO chapter specifies the model to be multicopy atomic — a store's visibility to all other harts is a single global event.

_catSupportComment: Whether each model is, can be, or cannot be specified in the cat language of herd7 (Alglave, Maranget & Tautschnig, 'Herding cats', TOPLAS 2014) — the de-facto lingua franca for machine-readable memory models. 'specified' = a cat model of this model exists (named in the note): one written for it, or one proved to define exactly its behaviours. 'expressible' = no cat model is published, but the model's allowed behaviours are a predicate on a single candidate execution over po/rf/co-derived relations, so a cat model could state it. 'not-expressible' = the model's verdict is not such a predicate — it quantifies over other executions (commit sequences, promise certificates, event-structure justifications), is computed denotationally over program syntax, or appeals to notions cat lacks (real time, liveness/eventual delivery). 'basis' records how the cell was decided: 'cat-model' = a concrete cat file was identified, 'cited' = the primary literature states the claim (an equivalence theorem, an authors' cat mechanisation, or the obstacle), 'extrapolated' = author judgement from the model's definitional style. Note the axis is expressiveness of the specification language, not model strength: 'not-expressible' is a statement about cat, not a defect of the model.

IMM.note: Declarative by construction: acyclicity and irreflexivity axioms over one candidate execution, mechanised in Coq. The axioms transcribe to cat directly, but no cat file accompanies the development.

Promising.note: A promise is legal only if the promising thread can certify it by a future thread-local execution, so whether one execution is allowed depends on other executions — not statable as a per-execution cat predicate. IMM was introduced precisely to give Promising a declarative over-approximation.

MRD.note: Dependencies are computed denotationally over an event structure that holds many conflicting executions at once; the verdict is not a filter on a single candidate execution. Checked by MoRDor rather than herd7.

sMRD.note: Same event-structure/denotational shape as MRD, with symbolic addresses on top; no per-candidate-execution predicate to encode in cat.

OD-LSO.note: The criterion is literally a cat axiom: acyclic(sb | rf).

OD-Dep.note: acyclic(dep | rf) over syntactic dependencies, which cat exposes as data/addr/ctrl.

OCaml.note: Defined operationally over per-location timestamped histories; the guarantees it delivers (coherence, SC atomics, local DRF) are per-execution conditions, but no cat rendering is published.

LKMM.note: linux-kernel.cat, maintained in the kernel tree (tools/memory-model) and run by herd7 — the model was written in cat from the start, with kernel.cfg/kernel.def shipped by herdtools7.

RVWMO.note: herd7's riscv.cat is the official RVWMO model distributed with the ISA manual (riscv-tso.cat for the Ztso extension).

PTX.note: Per-execution scoped axiomatic model, published as an executable Alloy formalisation; herd's bell/cat scope support (Alglave et al. 2015) makes a cat rendering routine, but none ships with the ISA spec.

TileIR.note: Axiomatic scoped model in the PTX lineage, specified in prose in the CUDA documentation; no machine-readable cat rendering is published.

AMDGPU.note: HSA-style scoped release consistency, specified in prose: the scoped-DRF guarantees are per-execution conditions that herd's bell/cat scopes can express, but no cat model is published.

OpenCL.note: The scoped OpenCL model is given in herd's bell/cat framework — scopes were added to cat for exactly this family (Alglave et al. 2015) — and run under herd7. The zoo's own scoped-GPU witnesses use herd7's plain C11 model as a proxy (cross-scope synchronisation degenerates to relaxed), not this cat model.

Vulkan.note: Khronos specifies the model executably in Alloy rather than cat. Its availability/visibility rules are per-execution constraints, expressible with cat's scope support.

CUDA.note: The C++-style scoped surface is layered on PTX's axiomatic model, so a cat rendering would follow PTX's; none is published at the CUDA level.

WebGPU.note: Derived from Vulkan's per-execution scoped model and specified in prose in the WGSL spec; no formal cat (or Alloy) artefact of its own.

Metal.note: Only informally specified. The documented guarantees (relaxed/acquire-release atomics, threadgroup and device barriers) are per-execution conditions a cat model could state, but there is no formal semantics to transcribe.

HRF.note: HRF-direct and HRF-indirect are conditions on a single execution (scoped races, scoped happens-before), which herd's bell/cat scope support expresses; the paper gives them in prose and set notation.

ScopedC11.note: A scoped generalisation of the C11 DRF framework: per-execution scoped happens-before and race conditions, expressible in scoped cat but not published as one.

Coherence.note: Run here as litmus/models/abstract-coherence.cat — cat's uniproc/scperloc axiom, acyclic(po-loc | com), on its own.

DRFx.note: SC-or-exception: cat states 'SC unless a race is flagged' with the same flag mechanism the C11 models use for data races. The region-serialisability enforcement is an implementation obligation, outside cat.

BMM.note: A TSO-style buffered abstract machine for Java; machines of this shape have equivalent per-execution axiomatic forms (as x86-TSO does with x86tso.cat), but none is published for BMM.

ClightTSO.note: Its consistency dimension is exactly TSO, which tso.cat/x86tso.cat state; the rest of the model (allocation, pointer arithmetic, undefined behaviour) is outside cat's event vocabulary, so no single cat model covers it.

RMMOA.note: A hierarchy of write buffers; the buffer discipline corresponds to a per-execution preserved-program-order plus coherence condition of PSO shape, but the model is presented purely operationally.

SRA.note: Four irreflexivity constraints over hb, mo and rf (irr-hb, strong-write-coherence, read-coherence, atomicity), all per-execution and all in cat's relational vocabulary; strong-write-coherence is just acyclic(hb | mo).

RA.note: As SRA but with write-coherence (mo;hb irreflexive) in place of strong-write-coherence — the release/acquire restriction of the vendored cpp11.cat and rc11.cat, and per-execution.

WRA.note: irr-hb, weak-read-coherence over hb|loc — cat states the per-location restriction of a relation directly — and the weakened RMW condition. Per-execution; mo is not used at all.

RAR.note: An operational reformulation of the RC11 release-acquire/relaxed fragment, proved to match it — and that fragment is what rc11.cat states.

ORC11.note: An operational presentation of RC11 built for RustBelt; the declarative RC11 it tracks is rc11.cat.

CRC.note: The underlying consistency model is a C11 fragment (release-acquire, SC fences, catch-fire non-atomics) that cat expresses; the compositional denotational layer is a reasoning device on top of it, not extra behaviour.

JAM.note: RC11-shaped acyclicity axioms over Java's access modes — essentially a relabelling of the fragment rc11.cat already states.

OHMM.note: An abstract machine with a global reorderable event buffer; the happens-before discipline it enforces is per-execution, but no declarative characterisation has been published.

Weakestmo.note: Built on event structures that hold several conflicting executions at once so speculation can be justified; the justification is not a property of the candidate execution being checked.

CSRA.note: The thread subsystem speculates over an event structure and commits under a rewriting discipline; allowedness depends on alternative executions, not on the single candidate execution cat sees.

WJES.note: Well-justification quantifies over alternative configurations of the event structure (a game-semantics style justification order), which no per-execution cat axiom captures.

LeakySemi.note: A denotational pomsets-with-predicate-transformers semantics computed compositionally over program syntax, not a filter on candidate executions. Its PwT-C11 instance does inherit RC11's top-level axioms, which cat states — but the dependency calculation that gives the model its content does not.

PwP.note: Semantic dependency is computed from logical preconditions carried by events during composition of the program's denotation, not read off a candidate execution.

GOS.note: Speculative steps are constrained by a stratification over possible future executions, so legality is not a per-execution condition.

JSMM.note: A C11-shaped axiomatic model (mechanised by Watt et al.): per-execution axioms over mixed-size accesses, which cat's mixed-size support (cf. x86tso-mixed.cat) already handles. No cat model has been published.

Wasm.note: Axiomatic and built on the C11 model — per-execution axioms plus byte-range accesses; expressible in mixed-size cat, though the spec's model is not given as one.

RMC.note: Executions carry programmer-declared ordering edges and the consistency condition is acyclicity of the induced visibility/execution orders — a per-execution axiom set, given in the paper as inference rules rather than cat.

RAO.note: Allowed behaviours are those obtainable by applying a sequence of program transformations to an SC execution: a rewriting derivation, not a predicate on the candidate execution.

TSC.note: Speculative computation is a reduction relation over program terms; which speculations are admissible is not a function of a single candidate execution.

EtE-SC.note: The programmer-visible model is SC, which sc.cat states exactly; the content of the proposal is the compiler and hardware enforcement, which cat does not describe.

VbD.note: Every access is volatile, so the model is SC over all accesses — sc.cat, with the interest lying in the implementation cost rather than the axioms.

SC-Haskell.note: Guarantees SC (sc.cat) for well-typed programs; the mechanism is the type discipline separating thread-local from shared state, not a weaker consistency predicate.

DeNovo.note: A coherence protocol plus a disciplined programming model rather than a consistency specification: the exposed guarantee is SC for the race-free, structured-parallel programs it targets, which sc.cat states.

DeNovoND.note: As DeNovo: the protocol is the artefact, and the guarantee exposed to the programmer (SC for disciplined, lock-using programs) is what a cat model would state.

DeNovoSync.note: As DeNovo: a coherence protocol supporting arbitrary synchronisation; the programmer-visible guarantee is SC for data-race-free programs, expressible in cat.

Spandex.note: A coherence interface for heterogeneous devices, not a consistency specification; the guarantee it preserves (SC for DRF, with scopes) is per-execution and expressible in scoped cat.

PC.note: Processor consistency is PRAM plus per-location coherence: both conjuncts are per-execution acyclicity conditions that cat states directly (cat's own scperloc axiom is the coherence half).

PRAM.note: Each process must see every other process's writes in issue order — a per-execution condition, with the per-process serialisations enumerable by cat's linearisations construct.

Causal.note: Causal memory is an acyclicity condition over the causal order (po union rf, transitively closed) together with per-process serialisations — all per-execution.

CC.note: AxCausal and AxCausalValue over an existentially quantified causal order, with a per-operation serialisation of that operation's causal past — the same shape as the Causal and CCv entries, and per-execution.

CCv.note: Causality plus a total arbitration order over all operations: an acyclicity condition on a single execution, and cat's co already supplies a per-location total order to carry the arbitration.

Slow.note: A per-execution constraint on which writes a read may return (own writes immediately, no earlier write by the same writer after a later one), directly statable as cat irreflexivity axioms.

Local.note: Only each process's own operations are constrained to appear in program order — a single per-execution axiom, weaker than cat's usual scperloc.

EC.note: Eventual delivery is a liveness property over infinite executions ('all but finitely many operations see a given write'). cat checks safety conditions on one finite candidate execution and has no way to state it.

CausalPlus.note: Causality plus convergence: convergence is the totality of the per-object arbitration order, which cat's co already provides. (The eventual-delivery assumption it inherits from the replicated setting is, as for EC, outside cat.)

RTCausal.note: The real-time condition — causally concurrent writes that do not overlap in real time must be ordered — refers to wall-clock intervals; cat's vocabulary has no notion of real time.

POCausal.note: The per-object causal order hbo = ((so & ob) | vis)+ is an acyclicity condition on a single execution, in cat's relational vocabulary.

RYW.note: Reading a session as a thread, the guarantee is a per-execution irreflexivity condition relating program order and visibility.

MR.note: A per-execution condition on one session's successive reads (the observed write set may not shrink), statable as a cat irreflexivity axiom over po and the communication relations.

MW.note: A per-execution ordering condition on a session's writes (per-session write order respected by every replica), i.e. a cat acyclicity axiom over po and co.

WFR.note: Session causality: writes of a session follow the writes their earlier reads observed — an acyclicity condition over po, rf and co on one execution.

x86-TSO+TM.note: Chong, Sorensen & Wickerson give the transactional extension in cat on top of the x86-TSO model, executable in their herd7 extension (and driven with memalloy to synthesise the validating litmus tests).

POWER+TM.note: The transactional rules are added in cat on top of ppc.cat and run in the authors' transaction-aware herd7.

ARMv8+TM.note: The proposed transactional rules are given in cat on top of the ARMv8 model and run in the authors' transaction-aware herd7.

PTSO.note: A declarative epoch-persistency axiom layered on TSO — per-execution, but persist and crash events are outside herd7's event vocabulary, so no cat model exists.

PARMv8.note: A declarative persist-order axiom layered on the ARMv8 consistency model (aarch64.cat); per-execution, but no cat model covers the persistency dimension.

C11+TM.note: The C++ TM technical specification is formalised in cat on top of RC11 and run in the authors' transaction-aware herd7.

DJR-SC.note: The framework is declarative: transactions are a per-execution axiom set parametric in the base model, so this instance is 'sc.cat plus transaction axioms'. No cat files accompany the paper.

DJR-TSO.note: Declarative transaction axioms over the TSO base model — per-execution, and expressible once transactional events are declared (as Chong et al. do in herd7); the paper gives no cat model.

DJR-ARMv8.note: Declarative transaction axioms over the ARMv8 base model — per-execution and cat-expressible, but published as inference rules rather than cat.

DJR-POWER.note: Declarative transaction axioms over the POWER base model — per-execution and cat-expressible, but published as inference rules rather than cat.

PSI.note: Declarative acyclicity axioms over transactional executions; a cat rendering needs transaction-class events (the extension Chong et al. added to herd7) but no additional expressive power.

SI.note: Declarative, timestamp-free acyclicity axioms over transactional executions — per-execution, and expressible in a transaction-aware cat.

PSER.note: Serialisability plus an orthogonal persist-order axiom: both are per-execution conditions, but no shipped cat model has crash/persist events.

Px86.note: A declarative persist-order axiom layered on x86-TSO; per-execution and cat-shaped, but herd7 has no persistency events.

PTSOsyn.note: Presented operationally with per-cache-line persistence buffers, alongside a declarative characterisation — per-execution modulo the persist events cat does not have.

PSC.note: An epoch-persistency dimension over SC, given declaratively as well as operationally; per-execution, but with persist events outside cat's vocabulary.

Px86view.note: Operational and view-based, but proved equivalent in Coq to the declarative Px86axiom, so it does have a per-execution characterisation — one no cat model states, for want of persist events.

Px86axiom.note: Declarative persistency axioms over x86-TSO executions; cat-shaped, but herd7 has no persist/crash events to express them over.

PEx86.note: Declarative model of x86 memory types and non-temporal stores plus persistency. The consistency half is mixed-size cat territory (x86tso-mixed.cat); the persist dimension is not part of any shipped cat model.

PArmv8view.note: Operational and view-based, but proved equivalent in Coq to the declarative PArmv8axiom, hence per-execution characterisable; no cat model covers persistency.

PArmv8axiom.note: Declarative persistency axioms over Armv8 executions (aarch64.cat plus a persist-order axiom in shape); no cat model exists for the persistency dimension.

PromisingARM.note: Despite its promise-based operational presentation, it is proved equivalent in Coq (for finite executions) to the axiomatic Armv8 and RVWMO models — that is, its behaviours are exactly those of herd7's aarch64.cat and riscv.cat. Unlike C/C++ Promising, its certification needs no value speculation.

_katSupportComment: Whether each model can be written in kater's input language (Kokologiannakis, Lahav & Vafeiadis, 'Kater', POPL 2023) — the fragment in which model comparison is decidable. Narrower than cat, and deliberately a separate axis from catSupport: kater requires consistency to be a conjunction of irreflexivity/emptiness constraints over regular expressions of base relations, so constructs cat states freely (notably intersections like po ∩ sameloc, which kater must first push into a regular form by an incomplete procedure) can put a cat-specified model outside it. 'specified' = a .kat definition exists (named in the note). 'expressible' = no .kat is published, but the model's axioms already have that shape. 'not-expressible' = they do not — the model quantifies over other executions, or needs constructs the fragment cannot state. 'basis': 'kat-model' = a concrete .kat file was identified, 'cited' = the primary literature states the claim, 'extrapolated' = author judgement from the model's definitional style. This map is partial by design: absence means not yet assessed, not 'no'. A model at either end of a 'kater'-provenance edge must appear here as 'specified' — check-consistency enforces it. Anything catSupport marks 'not-expressible' is outside this fragment too, since a per-execution predicate is a precondition for both.

SRA.note: Consistency is a conjunction of irreflexivity constraints over regular expressions of base relations — strong-write-coherence is irreflexive((hb | mo)+) — which is exactly kater's fragment. No .kat file is published, so it is expressible rather than specified.

RA.note: Same shape as SRA, with mo;hb in place of (hb | mo)+. Nothing here needs a construct outside kater's regular fragment.

SC.note: kater's kat/sc.kat: the single relation sc = po | rf | mo | fr, constrained acyclic.

TSO.note: kater's kat/tso.kat, with kat/tso-fm.kat as the Herding-cats-style flavour the two are proved equivalent to (paper Table 1, TSO ↔ TSOFM).

x86-TSO.note: Covered by kater's kat/tso.kat, which is the same rendering the zoo's by-construction TSO ≡ x86-TSO edge identifies. kat/pex86.kat is the persistency-extended Px86, not this node.

ARMv8.note: kater's kat/arm8.kat: dob/aob/bob ordering and acyclic(ob), with ISB and DMB.ST introduced as extra fence predicates.

POWER.note: kater ships kat/power-fm.kat and the simplified kat/power-fm-simpl.kat, kat/power-weak.kat and kat/power-fm-orig.kat. Three of them are unusable as comparison targets: power-weak, power-fm-simpl and power-fm-simpl-full carry the term eco*;po?;eco* in ar, and eco* contains the identity, so ar contains po and every containment into ar+ holds vacuously (checked: po <= power-weak::ar+ holds, where po <= tso::tso+ and po <= arm8::ob+ are both refuted). Only power-fm and power-fm-orig are non-degenerate, and against those the IMM compilation query is refuted on a fence-vocabulary gap. The paper notes the full model needs manual rotations to check within reasonable time (§3.7). See litmus/kater/open/compilation-IMM-vs-POWER.kat.

C11.note: kater's kat/c11-old.kat is the original C11 model of Batty et al. — the same node this row names.

RC11.note: kater's kat/rc11.kat (with kat/rc112.kat, an alternative formulation proved equivalent, and kat/rc11-genmc.kat for code export).

IMM.note: kater's kat/imm.kat (kat/imm-genmc.kat is the code-export variant).

LKMM.note: kater's kat/lkmm2.kat states LKMM's axioms in the fragment but is written over internal (-imm) relations, which kater rejects in every mode — including when that file is the one it was handed — so as shipped it is neither a comparison operand nor a checking target. The relations it redefines from their -imm counterparts (po, po-loc, mo, fr, rmw, ctrl, addr, data) are all in kater's builtin theory, so litmus/kater/derive-lkmm.sh restates it over those at run time; comparisons run against that derived file, not the shipped one. Its endpoints are untyped where IMM's are ([ACQ];po, not [R];(deps)+;[W]), which is what still blocks the LKMM compilation edges — see litmus/kater/open/compilation-LKMM-vs-x86-TSO.kat.
